Area · Core processes

Language

How we learn to speak, how we understand and produce sentences, non-verbal communication and bilingualism.

Level 1 · Short introduction

Language lets us combine a limited number of sounds and words to express an unlimited number of ideas. Children learn it astonishingly fast, without formal lessons, through interaction with the people around them. Psychology studies how it is acquired, how we understand and produce sentences and how it relates to thought.

Level 2 · Fuller explanation

How children learn to talk

  • First months: babies distinguish the sounds of all languages; around their first birthday they specialise in those of their surroundings.
  • Babbling at around 6–8 months and first words at around one year.
  • Vocabulary spurt in the second year, and two-word sentences ("more juice").
  • Grammar: between ages 2 and 5 revealing errors appear, such as "I goed" instead of "I went", which show that the child is applying rules and not just imitating.

Understanding and producing

When listening, the brain anticipates the next word and resolves ambiguities in fractions of a second. When speaking we make slips, such as swapping sounds around, that reveal how we plan sentences. The "tip of the tongue" phenomenon shows we can know a word's meaning without being able to reach its sound.

Non-verbal communication

Gestures, gaze, tone of voice and distance accompany words and sometimes contradict them. Sign languages are complete languages with their own grammar, and they are acquired through the same stages as spoken languages.

Bilingualism

Growing up with two languages does not confuse children or meaningfully delay their development. At first each vocabulary may be somewhat smaller, but the total is comparable.

Reading

All children learn to speak without formal teaching; reading is different. Writing is only about 5,000 years old, so the brain has not evolved to read: it repurposes existing areas. Research is clear that explicitly teaching the relationship between letters and sounds (phonics) is essential for most children. Dyslexia is a specific difficulty in that process and has nothing to do with intelligence.

Language and thought

Do we think in words? The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, in its strong version, said that language determines thought, and it has now been discarded. The weak version has some support: for example, Russian speakers, who have two basic words for light and dark blue, distinguish those shades a little faster. The influence exists but is modest.

Sign languages

Sign languages are complete languages with their own grammar, and they are processed in the same brain areas as spoken languages. A famous case is Nicaraguan Sign Language, created in the 1980s by deaf children who came together for the first time in special schools.

Talking to babies

In almost all cultures, adults speak to babies in a special way: higher pitch, exaggerated intonation, short sentences and repetition. Far from being a bad habit, this "infant-directed speech" captures their attention and helps them pick out words. Babies are also born able to distinguish the sounds of any language, but towards the end of the first year they specialise in those of their own. Janet Werker showed that six-month-old English-learning babies distinguished Hindi sounds they no longer distinguished at twelve months.

What is said without saying it

If someone asks "have you got the time?", they do not expect "yes". Pragmatics studies how we understand more than is literally said. The philosopher Paul Grice proposed that conversation rests on a cooperative principle: we assume the other person says what is necessary, true, relevant and clear. When they seem not to, we look for an implied meaning. This is how irony, hints and politeness work, and why these forms are harder for some autistic people and for those learning a foreign language.

When language is slow to come

About 7% of children have a developmental language disorder: they find it hard to learn to speak and understand, with no deafness, intellectual disability or other cause to explain it. It is much more common than people think and often goes unnoticed. Dyslexia, a specific difficulty in learning to read, affects between 5% and 10% depending on how it is defined. In both cases, early detection and support at school make a difference.

Level 3 · Going further, with references

In 1957 B. F. Skinner explained language as behaviour learned through reinforcement. Noam Chomsky responded in 1959 with a highly influential critique: children produce sentences they have never heard and learn from limited data, which suggested an innate capacity for grammar. Since then, usage-based approaches (Michael Tomasello) have shown that statistical learning and shared attention explain far more than was thought: 8-month-old babies already detect regularities in sequences of syllables.

Paul Broca (1861) and Carl Wernicke (1874) linked damage to specific areas of the left hemisphere to difficulties producing or understanding language (aphasias). Today we know language depends on broad networks in both hemispheres. Luria studied in depth the aphasias of soldiers wounded in the Second World War.

The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, that language determines thought, does not hold in its strong form. But there are more modest effects: for example, Russian speakers, who have two basic words for light and dark blue, distinguish those shades slightly faster.

Open debates: how much of the capacity for language is innate; what large language models teach us about how a language is learned; and the effects of bilingualism on executive control, which have turned out smaller and less consistent than first reported.

A language instinct?

Noam Chomsky proposed that humans are born with a specific capacity for language, a "universal grammar". Other researchers, such as Michael Tomasello, argue that children learn language with general abilities, such as detecting statistical patterns and understanding others' intentions. In 1996 Jenny Saffran showed that eight-month-old babies detected which syllables tended to go together after hearing just two minutes of a made-up language. The debate remains open.

Language and artificial intelligence

Large language models produce fluent text after being trained on enormous amounts of text. Their success has revived classic questions: how much of language can be learnt from statistics alone, and whether producing language amounts to understanding it. A child learns their language from thousands of times fewer words.

Silbo Gomero

On the island of La Gomera, a whistled language survives that turns Spanish into whistles and allows communication across ravines several kilometres apart. UNESCO declared it Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2009, and it is taught in the island's schools. In 2005, a study published in Nature found that in expert whistlers, hearing Silbo activates the same left-hemisphere language areas as speech, which does not happen in people who do not know it. To the brain, Silbo is language.

Seven thousand languages, many at risk

About seven thousand languages are spoken in the world, but half the population uses only about twenty. Many languages have few speakers, nearly all elderly, and may disappear this century. For psychology this is also a loss: almost all research on language has been done in a handful of languages, mostly English, and each different language allows ideas once thought universal to be tested.
